common_name: Valentine Bleeding Heart (Dark-Stemmed Deep Red Bleeding Heart)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in early spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, handling the brittle roots carefully and setting crowns just below the soil surface.

directions: Valentine is a Terra Nova Nurseries selection of old-fashioned bleeding heart bred for unusually dark, wine-red stems and leaf veins that set off intensely colored, deep crimson-red outer petals surrounding pure white inner petals — a richer, more saturated red than the soft pink typical of the species. Dangling, heart-shaped flowers line arching stems above blue-green, deeply cut foliage from mid-spring into early summer before the plant retreats into its usual summer dormancy as heat arrives. The darker stem and flower coloring reads especially well against pale companions such as hostas, ferns, or variegated Solomon's seal, and the plant shares the species' need for cool, humus-rich soil and reliable moisture during active growth. Divide congested clumps in early spring while still dormant to increase plantings or rejuvenate old stock.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries — Lamprocapnos spectabilis Valentine introduction notes

common_name: Burning Hearts Bleeding Heart (Red-and-White Silver-Foliage Dicentra)

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in early spring while dormant, keeping the fleshy roots shallow and well spread in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade.

directions: A Terra Nova Nurseries hybrid bred from the western native Dicentra formosa, Burning Hearts forms a tight mound of finely cut, silvery blue-gray, fern-like foliage that stays fresh-looking through the growing season rather than fading with summer heat the way old-fashioned bleeding heart does. Arching stems carry a long, heavy succession of vivid two-tone flowers — fiery red outer petals tipped in bright white — held well above the foliage from spring into fall wherever summers stay reasonably cool. Its compact habit and strong rebloom make it well suited to the front of a shaded border, a woodland path edge, or a container, paired with hostas, heucheras, or ferns. Provide humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil and afternoon shade, since foliage can scorch in hot, dry, or overly sunny sites.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries — Dicentra Burning Hearts introduction notes

common_name: Hewitt's Double Meadow Rue (Sterile Double-Flowered Yunnan Meadowrue)

planting.note: Divide established clumps carefully in early spring, or plant container specimens, in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; because the flowers are sterile, division or purchased stock is the only way to propagate true plants.

directions: Hewitt's Double is the classic old English selection of Yunnan meadowrue, bearing fully double, deep mauve-purple, pompon-like flowers that lack stamens entirely — the extra petals replace the pollen-bearing parts, so the sterile blooms never set seed and last considerably longer in the garden than the single-flowered species. Hundreds of the small double rosettes float on wiry, dark stems held well above delicate, blue-green, columbine-like compound foliage, creating an airy purple haze over the border from mid to late summer. Because the flowers are sterile, propagation is by division only, and established clumps resent disturbance, so plant it in a permanent, sheltered position with rich, consistently moist soil and light afternoon shade. Stake or grow among sturdy neighbors in windy sites, since the tall flowering stems can lean under the weight of the fully double blooms.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
